source: Synthetic Troubleshooting & Repair Reference Manual (ZS-authored stand-in, NOT Rockwell documentation)

sections.title: PCBA / Circuitry - Component Failure
steps: Power down and discharge the unit per lockout/tagout procedure before opening the enclosure.
Visually inspect the affected PCBA for obvious component damage: scorching, cracked packages, bulging/leaking electrolytic capacitors, lifted or cold solder joints.
Before re-energizing, check for shorts/continuity issues across primary power rails with a multimeter.
If a specific component is visually suspect, confirm with an in-circuit or out-of-circuit component test before replacing it.
Replace the failed component at the board level by reference designator where feasible, rather than the whole assembly.
Re-run the full functional test sequence against standard acceptance criteria before return to service.

sections.title: PCBA / Circuitry - Contamination
steps: Before addressing the board itself, inspect and remedy the contamination ingress path: enclosure door seals/gaskets and cooling-fan filtration.
Remove the affected PCBA and inspect for visible residue, corrosion, or conductive debris on traces and connector pins.

Clean per an approved electronics-safe, no-residue solvent procedure. Do not rely on compressed air alone if the contamination is conductive/particulate, since that can redistribute rather than remove it.
Inspect for corrosion-related trace damage under magnification before re-installing.
Re-test and monitor. If contamination recurs on the same unit, escalate the environmental root cause rather than repeatedly repairing the symptom.

sections.title: PCBA / Circuitry - Configuration Error
steps: Do not replace hardware. This is a configuration issue, not a component failure.
Verify the unit's firmware/parameter set against the current approved configuration baseline for its catalog/model.
Re-apply the correct configuration profile using the approved configuration tool, not manual field edits.
Document the incorrect configuration found, to support root-causing how it was introduced.
Re-run the full functional test after reconfiguration.

sections.title: PCBA / Circuitry - Worn / End of Life
steps: For a Worn/End-of-Life cause code on a PCB assembly, inspect electrolytic capacitors first (bulging, leaking, or discoloration at the vent) before assuming the whole board needs replacement.
Measure capacitance/ESR if test equipment is available and compare against nominal spec.
If capacitors test within spec, check other age-related wear points: connector contact oxidation, relay contact wear.
Replace only the confirmed worn component(s) where board-level rework is feasible.

sections.title: Motors - Worn / End of Life
steps: Check for audible or vibration signs of bearing wear before disassembly.
Measure shaft runout and bearing play against the motor's service-manual tolerance.
If an encoder/resolver is implicated, verify signal integrity and mounting alignment before replacing the sensor itself.
Replace bearings as a matched set, not individually, and re-grease per the motor's lubrication spec.
Re-test running current draw and vibration signature against baseline after reassembly.

sections.title: Fan / Cooling - Worn / End of Life
steps: For a Worn/End-of-Life cause code on a fan assembly, check first for elevated bearing noise/vibration and reduced RPM under load: the classic signature of fan-bearing wear.
Verify airflow/RPM against the unit's rated spec. A worn fan often still spins but underperforms before it fully seizes.
Do not attempt to lubricate sealed fan bearings not designed for field relubrication. Replace the fan assembly as a unit once wear is confirmed.

Where available, check the fan's duty-cycle/runtime hours against its rated service life to distinguish premature failure (investigate airflow/temperature root cause) from expected end-of-life wear-out.
After replacement, verify airflow/RPM against spec before closing up the unit.

sections.title: Fan / Cooling - Component Failure
steps: Determine whether the failure is mechanical (bearing/blade) or electrical (drive circuitry) before replacing the whole fan assembly.
For a suspected mechanical failure, check for physical obstruction, blade damage, and bearing freeplay.
For a suspected electrical failure, verify fan drive voltage is present at the connector before condemning the fan motor itself.
Replace the fan assembly as a unit if the motor has failed; if only the drive circuit failed, board-level repair may be possible (see Section 1).
After replacement, verify airflow/RPM against spec before closing up the unit.

sections.title: HMI / Display - Worn / End of Life
steps: For touchscreen wear-out symptoms (reduced sensitivity, dead zones), clean the surface and check for protective-film degradation before assuming a hardware failure.
Test touch response across the full surface in a diagnostic/calibration mode if available.
For display backlight dimming, compare against a known-good unit's brightness rather than subjective judgment alone.
Replace the touchscreen/display assembly as a unit. Field-level component repair is not typically supported at this level.

general.title: General troubleshooting protocol
steps: General Troubleshooting Protocol applies. Proceed with standard electrical/mechanical baseline checks.
